title: Data classes and shallow copies
summary: If copy instead receives topics = first.topics.toMutableList(), what prints?
explanation:
A data class generates useful operations such as equals, hashCode and copy from properties declared in its primary constructor. Properties declared only in the body are excluded from those generated comparisons and copies. copy(topics = newList) replaces that constructor property in the new instance. toMutableList() copies a list container, but its element references are still shared.

Calling toMutableList on a list returns a new mutable outer list containing the same element references. Here adding to the copied container leaves the original container at one element; this is not a recursive clone.
```kotlin
fun main() {
    val original = mutableListOf("read")
    val copied = original.toMutableList()
    copied.add("write")
    println("${original.size} ${copied.size}")
}
```
Expected output: 1 2.

copy creates another data-class instance but does not recursively clone referenced mutable objects. Here both instances retain the same MutableList reference. Read-only val prevents replacing the reference, not modifying that list.

```kotlin
fun main() {
    val first = Plan(mutableListOf("C"))
    val second = first.copy()
    second.topics.add("Kotlin")
    println(first.topics.size)
}
```

title: Extensions use static resolution

```kotlin
    val narrow: Detail = Detail()
    println(broad.label())
    println(narrow.label())
```

title: Files and explicit encodings

title: JVM dates and time zones
summary: If the instant becomes 12:30 UTC on the same day, what dates print?
explanation:
The JVM java.time.Instant represents a point on the time line. ZoneId supplies rules for presenting that instant as local calendar time. Converting with atZone preserves the instant, not necessarily its displayed date.

Instant.parse takes ISO instant text such as "2025-01-01T00:30:00Z" and returns an Instant; Z identifies UTC. ZoneId.of takes a zone-ID String such as "UTC" or "America/New_York" and returns the corresponding ZoneId rules object. These are the inputs to the existing atZone calls.

At 00:30 UTC on January 1, New York is still on December 31. toLocalDate extracts the date from each zoned representation. This example uses JVM java.time rather than claiming a multiplatform date API or reading the current clock.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

fun main() {
    val instant = Instant.parse("2025-01-01T00:30:00Z")
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("UTC")).toLocalDate())
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")).toLocalDate())
}
```

Expected output or behavior: 2025-01-01
2024-12-31. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
